newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan debates virtues of aid, mulls cuts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan debates virtues of aid, mulls cuts.

text.p: Japan, the world's biggest provider of foreign aid, is questioning its policies to the developing world.
A heated debate has included calls for the previously unthinkable -- budget cuts.

Since 1991, Japan has topped the list of donor countries in terms of the amount of money spent, although it has fallen back in the rankings when figures are given as a percentage of gross national product (GNP).

Official development assistance (ODA) grew in leaps and bounds from the late 1970s as resource-poor Japan saw the need to strengthen friendships with resource-rich developing nations and to boost its contribution to the international community to match its economic power.
A TIME OF FISCAL REFORM
But growth has slowed in recent years and now the Japanese are finding their pockets are not as deep as they used to be.
Beleagured by debt and with a rapidly ageing population that could mean crippling tax burdens in the future, the government has made slashing the deficit its paramount priority.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has declared no area immune from budget cuts and Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda has set up a panel to review aid, stating that new ODA policy should focus on "quality not quantity".
Many predict that Japan's self-imposed goal to spend between $70 and $75 billion in foreign aid between 1993 and 1997 will be one of the first casualties in the war on spending.
It is a goal the Japanese already know they cannot meet. In 1996, aid fell 35 percent in dollar terms, bringing total ODA over the past four years to $49.2 billion.
The weaker yen and rising loan repayments from recipient countries on past long-term aid loans were responsible for the fall in net aid disbursements, officials said.

Domestic newspapers have also reported that officials from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party and its political allies on the government's fiscal reform panel have agreed to ODA budget cuts for the next business year.
EXPERTS SEE LARGE CUTS UNLIKELY
Experts, however, say cuts are unlikely and even if they do happen they are likely to be extremely modest.

"It's about Japan keeping up its image with developing countries. Japan has to say that ODA is important. Japan, unlike the U.S. or Europe, is highly dependent on developing countries," said Jun Nishikawa, an economics professor at Waseda University.
Aid, experts say, is the only true instrument of foreign policy that Japan, restricted militarily by its constitution, possesses.

Aid has lent strength to Japan's aspirations to join the United Nations Security Council and contributed indirectly to the placement of Japanese such as U.N. Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi, they add.
But budget cuts are only one aspect of the aid debate.

Criticism ranges from lack of a coherent policy, a bureaucratic structure spanning 19 agencies and lack of technical skill, especially in the field, to too much emphasis on infrastructural projects and not enough support for non-governmental organisations.

The sense that Japan is no longer the economic power it once was has also meant a growing willingness to come out and say that aid programmes should not just be made on humanitarian grounds but should also serve national interests.
BUSINESS LOBBY PUSHES FOR BIGGER SLICE OF THE PIE
The business lobby, in particular, has decried the small number of ODA contracts landed by Japanese firms and called for the government to reconsider some partial tying of loans.
Japan's ODA loans are mostly untied, meaning the recipients are not required to spend the money on Japanese goods.

The untying process began in the late 1970s after criticism that Japan's aid programme only served to promote exports. Since then the percentage of aid loan contracts landed by Japanese firms has dwindled to 27 percent.
"Japanese taxes are flowing overseas without providing work for Japanese firms," said a spokesman for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, a firm which specialises in power plant projects.
Foreign counterparts are not without sympathy for this view, saying that in the current climate of donor fatigue, realistic policies have to be taken.
"For every donor country, be it the U.S. or Japan, somehow their business community needs to benefit," said Myles Elledge of Development Alternatives, a U.S. firm that works in Japanese ODA.
PERU HOSTAGE CRISIS HELPS SHIFT TO QUALITY

The government's shift to an emphasis on "quality" in its aid policy has also been given fresh impetus in the wake of a four-month rebel occupation of the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru. The siege ended on April 22 when Peruvian commandos stormed the building.
The Marxist rebels who took over the ambassador's residence in Lima said they had chosen Japan as a target "due to the constant meddling of Japan in Peru".
"The Peru incident has made people look below the surface to see where ODA is going," said Waseda University's Nishikawa.
Foreign Ministry officials emphasise that the essential role of aid within Japan's foreign policy will not change.

"There are all sorts of expectations for grants, loans and technical cooperation from Japan and answering these expectations is necessary as part of Japan's international contribution," said Masahiko Horie, director of the Foreign Ministry's aid policy division.
Global issues such as AIDS, the environment and population problems only mean demand for aid is growing, he said.
"In developing countries there are still over one billion people who have no choice but to live in extreme poverty," he added.
